ledger.sentence: An ultrasound scan uses high-frequency sound waves to make a picture of the inside of the body.
ledger.note: Search text: probe emits high-frequency sound waves, echoes from body structures converted into a moving image.

ledger.sentence: The sound waves bounce off different parts of the body, and the echoes are picked up by a probe and turned into a moving image.
ledger.note: Same: sound waves reflect off structures; computer builds picture; moving image.

ledger.sentence: It does not use radiation or X-rays.
ledger.note: NHS: ultrasound scans do not use radiation, unlike X-rays or CT.

ledger.sentence: NHS and NHS trust pages describe ultrasound being used to look inside the body, to guide procedures such as biopsy and drainage, and during pregnancy.
ledger.note: Retrieved NHS text covered pregnancy scans and guidance of biopsy/drainage, not the three-part statement attributed to NHS pages.

ledger.sentence: It can also help to guide a biopsy or the draining of fluid.
ledger.note: Royal Marsden: biopsy performed under ultrasound guidance; image-guided drainage of fluid or abscess uses ultrasound or CT guidance.

ledger.sentence: Gel is put on the skin over the area and a small probe is moved across it.
ledger.note: Gel on skin and probe moved across skin supported; sonographer/radiologist watching pictures not stated verbatim.

ledger.sentence: The gel is water-based and washes off easily, and trust leaflets say it will not stain clothing.
ledger.note: Trust text: water-based gel, wipe off with paper towel, one trust says it dissolves in water and will not stain clothing.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says an ultrasound scan takes around 10 to 45 minutes, and may take longer.
ledger.note: NHS page says around 10 to 45 minutes, possibly longer; trusts give 10 to 30 minutes. About 20 minutes not found.

ledger.sentence: Afterwards the gel can be wiped off and the person can get dressed.
ledger.note: Wipe gel off and get dressed supported; leaving straight away not stated.

ledger.sentence: For pelvic and bladder scans, people are usually asked to arrive with a full bladder.
ledger.note: Full bladder supported for pelvic and bladder scans (trust pages: drink water, do not empty bladder). Kidneys were listed under fasting, not full bladder.

ledger.sentence: Trust leaflets explain that a full bladder gives a clearer picture because sound waves travel more easily through fluid.
ledger.note: Retrieved reason: sound waves travel more easily through fluid (urine), giving a clearer picture. Womb positioning not found.

ledger.sentence: Leaflets ask people not to empty their bladder until after the scan, and say a toilet is nearby afterwards.
ledger.note: Retrieved: do not empty bladder until after the scan; full bladder may be a little uncomfortable; toilet nearby afterwards. Leaving mid-scan not found.

ledger.sentence: Scans of some organs, such as the liver, may need no food for several hours beforehand.
ledger.note: Search: for abdominal scans (liver, gallbladder, kidneys) people are usually asked not to eat for several hours.

ledger.sentence: The hospital or clinic tells people how to prepare for their type of scan.
ledger.note: Retrieved: the hospital or clinic should tell you how to prepare. Appointment letter specifically not confirmed.

ledger.sentence: The usual scan is external, with the probe on the skin.
ledger.note: Trust pages: external scan with probe moved across the skin; transvaginal is the internal alternative.

ledger.sentence: Some people have a transvaginal (internal) scan.
ledger.note: Transvaginal scans exist and are used more in early pregnancy; "more information about the pelvis" not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: For this scan the probe is disinfected, covered with a protective sheath and lubricated with gel.
ledger.note: Trusts: probe cleaned, covered with protective sheath, lubricated with jelly/gel.

ledger.sentence: People usually need to empty their bladder first for an internal scan.
ledger.note: Several trusts say to empty the bladder first for a transvaginal scan.

ledger.sentence: Ultrasound can also be used to look at blood flow and at whether blood vessels are narrowed or blocked.
ledger.note: Royal Marsden: ultrasound can detect blood flow and any narrowing or blockage of blood vessels.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says the sound waves used in ultrasound scans are safe, and that ultrasound scans do not use radiation.
ledger.note: NHS says the sound waves are safe and ultrasound uses no radiation; "low risk" wording not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: An NHS maternity leaflet says scans are painless and have no known side effects.
ledger.note: An NHS maternity leaflet says scans are painless with no known side effects; NHS says no known risks from the sound waves. Not stated on the cited nhs.uk pregnancy page in retrieved text.

ledger.sentence: One hospital notes that standard ultrasound gel is not sterile, so there is a very small risk of infection in some circumstances.
ledger.note: Retrieved: standard gel is not sterile so there is a very small risk of infection in some circumstances. Skin irritation and prevention by wiping not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: People with a latex allergy are asked to tell the department beforehand so latex-free products can be used.
ledger.note: NHS: people with a latex allergy should tell staff so an alternative can be used.

ledger.sentence: The images are reviewed by the specialist who carried out the scan.
ledger.note: Royal Marsden leaflet: images reviewed by the specialist who performed the exam; sonographer/radiologist wording not confirmed.

ledger.sentence: The report goes to the doctor or team who requested the scan.
ledger.note: Search: result is sent to the doctor who referred you for the scan.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says results may be given at the end of the appointment, or can take a few weeks, depending on the reason for the scan.
ledger.note: NHS: results may be given at the end of the appointment or take a few weeks depending on the reason for the scan; one trust says within 1 week for GP referrals. 24 hours not found.

ledger.sentence: An ultrasound scan uses sound waves rather than radiation, and the NHS describes the sound waves used as safe.
ledger.note: Sound waves not radiation supported; "low risk" not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: A water-based gel goes on the skin, and a small probe is moved over the area being scanned.
ledger.note: Water-based gel and probe moved over skin supported.

ledger.sentence: Pelvic and bladder scans usually need a full bladder, and the hospital or clinic explains how to prepare.
ledger.note: Full bladder supported for pelvic and bladder scans only; appointment letter not confirmed.

ledger.sentence: Some people have an internal (transvaginal) scan.
ledger.note: Transvaginal scan exists; purpose "to give more information" not retrieved.
